coreTruths.title: Local anaesthetic safety is governed by weight-based dose ceilings, not cartridge counts
coreTruths.broaderContext: Local anaesthesia is the most-used drug intervention in dentistry. Its safety record rests on respecting maximum doses per kilogram, recognising toxicity, and choosing agents to fit the patient.
coreTruths.body:
## Maximum dose is per kilogram, and adrenaline raises the ceiling

The most commonly used preparation is 2% lidocaine with 1:80,000 adrenaline. Maximum dose is 3mg/kg lidocaine plain and 7mg/kg with adrenaline [1]. The vasoconstrictor slows systemic absorption, which is what lets the ceiling rise. A small adult easily reaches the limit on routine extractions if cartridges are stacked without thinking.

## Each agent has its own ceiling and quirks

Prilocaine with octapressin tops out at 600mg in an adult, around 8 cartridges of 2.2mL, and can cause methaemoglobinaemia in excess [2]. Bupivacaine is long-acting (6h plain, 8h with adrenaline) and useful for post-operative analgesia, but the maximum is only 2mg/kg [3]. Articaine 4% with 1:100,000 adrenaline is now widely used and is at least as effective as lidocaine [4]. Knowing the ceiling for each agent matters more than knowing the brand.

## Toxicity can present late and the signs are neurological before they are cardiac

Toxicity may appear some time after the injection [5]. Early signs are circumoral numbness, dizziness, metallic taste, and visual or auditory disturbance, escalating to agitation, loss of consciousness with tonic-clonic convulsions, and cardiovascular collapse [6]. A patient who feels strange ten minutes after a block is not necessarily anxious. Pure LA allergy is rare; once preservative reactions are excluded, true allergy probably does not exist [7].

## Topicals are useful but carry their own risks

Lidocaine spray or paste is the workhorse topical, but frequent skin exposure causes contact eczema, so it should not be applied with bare fingers [8]. EMLA, a eutectic mix of lidocaine and prilocaine, is the standard skin topical for venepuncture in children, applied 30 minutes before under an occlusive dressing [9].

citations.quote: Most commonly used preparation (2% lidocaine 1:80,000 adrenaline), gives effective pulpal analgesia for 1.5h and altered soft tissue sensation for up to 3h. Extremely safe; maximum dose 3mg/kg lidocaine without adrenaline, 7mg/kg with adrenaline.
Similar but slightly less duration and effect compared to lidocaine/adrenaline. May cause methaemoglobinaemia in excess. Maximum safe dose (adult) 600mg (8 × 2.2mL cartridges).
Long-acting LA (6h plain, 8h with adrenaline); useful as a post-operative analgesic. Maximum safe dose 2mg/kg. Only available in ampoules. Levobupivacaine is a similar drug.
This is now widely used (4% articaine 1:100,000 adrenaline) At least as effective as lidocaine; said to diffuse through bone better. No hard evidence of superiority.

Any clinician administering local anaesthetic should be aware of the signs of toxicity and understand its immediate management. It is important to note that local anaesthetic toxicity may occur some time after the initial injection.

Circumoral numbness. Dizziness/lightheadedness. Metallic taste. Drowsiness and disorientation. Visual and auditory disturbances. Sudden alteration in mental status. Severe agitation or loss of consciousness with or without tonic–clonic convulsions. Cardiovascular collapse.
Adverse reaction to LA is a C/I, but in reality once allergy to preservatives in the solution is excluded, LA allergy probably does not exist.

Lidocaine is the only really useful topical analgesic among those just listed. It is available as a spray or a paste which is applied to mucosa several minutes prior to injecting. There is a high incidence of contact eczema in people frequently exposed to these preparations, so do not apply with bare fingers.

EMLA® cream, a eutectic mix of lidocaine and prilocaine, is an invaluable skin topical analgesic, used prior to venepuncture in children. Apply to puncture site and cover with Opsite® or equivalent dressing for at least 30min.

coreTruths.title: Effective regional blocks depend on bony landmarks, not soft-tissue feel
coreTruths.broaderContext: Block anaesthesia targets a nerve where it is constrained by bone. Reliable success comes from knowing the anatomy of the foramen, not from chasing the patient's lip-numb sensation.
coreTruths.body:
## Infiltrations rely on diffusion through periosteum and bone

The aim of an infiltration is to deposit LA supraperiosteally as close to the apex as possible, then let it diffuse through periosteum and bone to the nerves entering the apex [1]. That is why dense compact bone, especially in the adult mandible, can stop a properly given infiltration from working, and a regional or intraligamentary technique becomes the fallback [2].

## The IDB targets the lingula, with the needle laterally to the pterygomandibular raphe

For an inferior alveolar block, the patient's mouth has to be wide open. With the thumb in the retromolar fossa, the needle enters at the midpoint of the thumb tip slightly above the occlusal plane, lateral to the pterygomandibular raphe. After about 0.5cm a small amount goes in for the lingual nerve, the syringe is rotated about 40 degrees across the dorsum of the tongue, and the needle is advanced to bone at the lingula before the rest is deposited [3]. The needle should never go in to the hub. The mandibular foramen sits relatively higher in the edentulous mandible, which moves the entry point with it [4].

## Soft-tissue numbness does not mean pulpal anaesthesia

Soft tissue analgesia is reached at lower nerve-fibre concentrations than pulpal analgesia [5]. A numb lip is the early sign that the block is taking, not proof that the tooth is anaesthetised. Pulpal anaesthesia takes several minutes longer and wears off first, usually within an hour of standard lidocaine with adrenaline [6]. Drilling the moment the lip tingles is how reliable blocks get a reputation for being unreliable.

## Failure has predictable causes worth running through before reinjecting

When a block fails the usual culprits are poor technique with inadequate volume, injection into muscle (which causes self-resolving trismus), injection into infected tissue, intravascular placement, dense bone, or anastomosis from neighbouring nerves [7]. Reinjecting more of the same without thinking through which of these applies just doubles the dose without improving the odds.

citations.quote: The aim is to deposit LA supraperiosteally in as close proximity as possible to the apex of the tooth to be anaesthetized. The LA will diffuse through periosteum and bone to bathe the nerves entering the apex.
Dense compact bone can prevent a properly given infiltration from working. Counter by using intraligamentary or regional LA.

With the palpating thumb lying in the retromolar fossa, the needle should be inserted at the midpoint of the tip of the thumb slightly above the occlusal plane lateral to the pterygomandibular raphe. The needle is inserted ~0.5cm and if a lingual nerve block is required, 0.5mL of LA is injected at this point. The syringe is then moved horizontally ~40° across the dorsum of the tongue and advanced to make contact with the lingula. Once bony contact is made the needle is withdrawn slightly and the remainder of the LA injected.

Note that the mandibular foramen varies in position with age (for children, see …… Local analgesia for children, p. 82). In the edentulous, the foramen, and hence the point of needle insertion, is relatively higher than in the dentate.

Soft tissue analgesia is more easily obtained, needing a lower degree of penetration of solution into nerve bundles, than does analgesia from pulpal stimulation. A numb lip does not therefore indicate pulpal anaesthesia.

Concentration of analgesic ↑ rapidly around the nerve at first and provides soft tissue analgesia; however, this is reached substantially before the levels needed for pulpal analgesia, which takes several minutes and will wear off first (usually within an hour of a standard lidocaine/adrenaline LA).

Poor technique and inadequate volume of LA. Injection into a muscle (will result in trismus which resolves spontaneously). Injection into an infected area (which should not be done anyway as this risks spreading the infection). Intravascular injection; clearly of no analgesic benefit. Small amounts of intravascular LA cause few problems. Toxicity, …… Other drug reactions and interactions, p. 564. Dense compact bone can prevent a properly given infiltration from working. Counter by using intraligamentary or regional LA. Infrequently, anastomosis from either aberrant or normal nerve fibres not transmitted with a blocked nerve bundle.

coreTruths.title: Conscious sedation is defined by a single drug, titrated, with the patient still rousable
coreTruths.broaderContext: Sedation in dentistry sits between local anaesthesia and general anaesthesia. Its safety record depends on a tight definition: one drug, titrated, an awake patient, and protective reflexes intact.
coreTruths.body:
## The Poswillo definition draws the line

Sedation was redefined by the Poswillo Committee as the single injection of a single drug, and in IV outpatient sedation that single injection must be titrated and incremental [1]. The principal recommendations make it explicit: IV sedation should use one drug with a single titrated dose to an endpoint remote from anaesthesia, and sedation should be preferred to GA whenever possible [2]. Mixing drugs or chasing depth turns conscious sedation into something else with very different risks.

## Sedation means an awake patient with reflexes intact

Sedation is an altered level of consciousness in which the patient, although awake, has a reduced level of fear and anxiety [3]. The aim with relative analgesia is a comfortable, relaxed, awake patient who can open their mouth on request, with no loss of consciousness or laryngeal reflex [4]. With IV midazolam the same rule holds: loss of the laryngeal reflex is oversedation and means stopping, securing the airway, and only proceeding once respiration and protection are confirmed [5].

## Titration replaces fixed dosing

With RA, oxygen runs at 100% first, then nitrous oxide is built up in 10% steps each held for a minute. Most patients settle at 20-30% [6]. With IV midazolam, a 2-3mg bolus of diazepam or 1-2mg of midazolam goes in, then further 1mg increments after waiting a minute, until adequate sedation is reached [7]. Midazolam is the drug of choice: water-soluble, roughly twice the strength of diazepam, much shorter half-life with no significant metabolites, and more amnesic [8]. Itchy nose is an early sign of full sedation, hiccups mean overshoot [9].

## Monitoring, escort, and reversal are non-negotiable

A second appropriate person trained in CPR must be present, with pulse, BP, and mandatory pulse oximetry [10]. The patient must be escorted home and forbidden to drive or take responsible roles for 24 hours [11]. Flumazenil is the specific reversal agent, but its half-life is shorter than the drugs it reverses, so multiple doses may be needed and a reversed patient is never left unsupervised [12]. Poswillo also reserves flumazenil for emergencies, not routine reversal at the end of an ordinary case [13].

## Patient selection: not children, not the unescorted, not the unstable

IV sedation in children should be approached with caution, and benzodiazepines are not recommended under 16 because of resistance and paradoxical stimulation [14]. Relative contraindications include needle phobia, the patient who cannot be accompanied or who needs to drive or care for children within 24 hours, liver or renal impairment, glaucoma, psychoses, pregnancy, or benzodiazepine allergy [15]. Elderly patients are very sensitive: doses are halved over 60 [16].

citations.quote: Its report redefined ‘sedation’ as the ‘single injection of a single drug’. In terms of IV sedation in an out-patient setting this is the surest way to avoid problems provided the ‘single injection’ is titrated and incremental.

Sedation be used in preference to GA whenever possible. For sedation by inhalation, the minimum concentration of O2 be fixed at 30%. Flumazenil be reserved for emergency use. IV sedation be limited to the use of one drug with a single titrated dose to an endpoint remote from anaesthesia.
An altered level of consciousness in which the patient, although awake, has a ↓ level of fear and anxiety.
To produce a comfortable, relaxed, awake, patient who is able to open their mouth on request with no loss of consciousness or the laryngeal reflex.
Loss of laryngeal reflex constitutes oversedation and means you must stop and ensure the airway is patent, only proceeding if there is no respiratory depression and the airway can be protected.

Start by delivering 100% O2 via a nasal mask and set flow control to match their tidal volume (flow rates 6–8L/min for adult, 4L/min for child). Then give 10% nitrous oxide for 1min, ↑ (if needed) to 20% for 1min, ↑ to 30% (if needed) for 1min, and so on. Most patients achieve adequate levels of sedation at 20–30%; some may require less, a few rather more.
Place the patient in the supine position and give a small bolus (2–3mg diazepam, 1–2mg midazolam). Wait for 1min and then give further increments until adequate level of sedation is achieved.

A water-soluble benzodiazepine of roughly double the strength of diazepam. Has a much shorter half-life, with no significant metabolites, creating a quicker and smoother recovery, and it is more amnesic than diazepam. It is supplied in 5mL ampoules, containing 5mg midazolam, allowing 1mg/increment. Drug of choice.
An itchy nose is an early sign of ‘complete’ sedation. Hiccups constitute oversedation.
A ‘second appropriate person’ must be present. Pulse and BP should be monitored. Pulse oximetry is mandatory.
Allow time for recovery (30–60min) in calm surroundings. The patient must be accompanied home and forbidden to drive or assume a responsible position for 24h.

A specific benzodiazepine reversal agent. Dose: 200 micrograms IV over 15sec followed by 100 micrograms at 60sec intervals until reversal occurs. NB: this drug has a shorter half-life than the drugs it will reverse, therefore multiple doses may be required. Patients should never be reversed and then left unsupervised.
Flumazenil be reserved for emergency use.
Interestingly, children show not only resistance to these drugs but sometimes paradoxical stimulation, and benzodiazepine sedation is not recommended for the <16s.

an inexperienced operator, or a patient with needle phobia, form relative C/Is. As do inability to be accompanied, the need to be in a responsible position within 24h of sedation (e.g. looking after young children on own, driving, etc.), patients with liver or renal impairment, glaucoma, psychoses, pregnancy, or a demonstrated allergy to the benzodiazepines.
Elderly patients tend to be very sensitive to benzodiazepines and doses are best halved in the >60yrs age group initially.

coreTruths.title: Nitrous oxide is fast-on, fast-off, but its safety needs scavenging and an oxygen floor
coreTruths.broaderContext: Relative analgesia is the workhorse paediatric and dental-anxiety sedation. Its kinetics make it forgiving, but its toxicity to staff and to vulnerable patients sets the boundaries.
coreTruths.body:
## The pharmacology is what makes RA forgiving

Nitrous oxide does not enter metabolic pathways and is distributed as a poorly soluble solution. Peak saturation is reached within 5 minutes and 90% is eliminated within 10 minutes [1]. That kinetic profile is what allows real-time titration and rapid recovery, and it is why patients leave the chair safe to walk out within 10 minutes after a 2-minute oxygen flush [2].

## Best fit is anxious patients and children doing atraumatic work

RA is particularly valuable in anxious patients undergoing relatively atraumatic procedures and in children, for whom benzodiazepines are less suitable [3]. The analgesic effect itself only kicks in at high concentrations, so the value to the dentist is mainly the sedative effect plus reassuring patter, which is why some operators describe the technique as hypnosedation [4].

## Oxygen floor and scavenging are the two safety rules

An RA machine will not deliver less than 30% oxygen, and Poswillo fixed that minimum [5]. Scavenging is essential because nitrous oxide accumulation can lead to vitamin B12 deficiency and demyelination, with a real hazard to pregnant staff in confined spaces [6]. The patient also gets oxygenated with 100% O2 for two minutes at the end before being moved to recovery [2].

## A short list of contraindications, headed by pregnancy and upper-airway obstruction

Contraindications are few but include upper airway obstruction such as a cold, pregnancy (teratogenicity and miscarriage risk), and pre-existing vitamin B12 deficiency. Confirming the date of the last menstrual period before use is good practice [7]. Nausea and vomiting can also occur during a session [7].

citations.quote: It is an inert gas which does not enter any of the body’s metabolic pathways and is distributed as a poorly soluble solution. This allows very rapid distribution; peak saturation is reached within 5min and is similarly eliminated (90% in 10min).

To discontinue, turn flow to 100% O2 and oxygenate patient for 2min. Then remove mask and get the patient to sit in a recovery room for 10min, by which time 90% of nitrous oxide will have been blown off and they will be safe to leave the surgery.
It is of particular value in anxious patients undergoing relatively atraumatic procedures and in children, for whom the benzodiazepines are less suitable.
Remember that RA relies on the reassuring banter of the operator more than any of the other sedation techniques, and many view this as hypnosedation.
For sedation by inhalation, the minimum concentration of O2 be fixed at 30%.

This is the major problem associated with RA. It is essential to have a scavenging system in place as nitrous oxide accumulation can lead to vitamin B12 deficiency and demyelination syndromes. There is a real potential hazard to pregnant staff working in confined conditions with this gas.

Few, but include upper airway obstruction, e.g. a cold. Pregnancy (risk of teratogenicity and miscarriage to both the patient and staff), first trimester makes the procedure difficult and pre-existing vitamin B12 deficiency would C/I its use. It is good practice to confirm the date of the last menstrual period and/or risk of pregnancy prior to use. Other C/I, e.g. complex medical history, are relative and may limit nitrous oxide use in practice but not in hospital. There is also a risk of nausea and vomiting when using nitrous oxide gas.

coreTruths.title: General anaesthesia in dentistry is a hospital procedure with a shared airway, never a practice convenience
coreTruths.broaderContext: Since the 2001 GDC ruling, GA for dentistry has been pulled out of practice and into hospital. The reason is the shared airway, which makes any dental GA inherently higher-risk than other surgery.
coreTruths.body:
## GA is a triad, not just sleep

General anaesthesia is a triad of unconsciousness, muscle relaxation, and analgesia [1]. None of those three is delivered by a single drug at a single dose. That is why GA needs an anaesthetist with specialist training, not a dentist who has done a course.

## The shared airway is the fundamental problem

The surgeon and the anaesthetist both need access to the same anatomical site [2]. That is why hospital dental GA usually means nasoendotracheal intubation, muscle relaxation, and ventilation, with a throat pack to supplement the cuff that must be removed at the end [2]. The major risk of intubation is intubating the oesophagus and not recognising it [3]. The LMA is a common alternative for short day-case extractions but does not protect against aspiration, so patients still have to be starved [4].

## GA in primary dental care has effectively been abolished

Since the GDC's 2001 amendment, the administration of GAs in a dental practice setting has been effectively abolished in the UK [5]. The 2009 GDC recommendations reinforced this: dental treatment under GA must only happen in a hospital setting that has critical-care facilities, and a referrer who breaches these recommendations is liable to a charge of serious professional misconduct [6]. GA may only be given by an anaesthetist on the GMC specialist register, a supervised trainee, or a non-consultant career-grade anaesthetist under named consultant supervision [7].

## Fasting, history, and a list of red-flag conditions

Most anaesthetists require at least 6 hours fasting after food and 4 hours after fluid [8]. Hospital admission is preferred for cardiovascular or respiratory disease (especially MI within 6 months), anaemia or sickle disease, severe liver or renal impairment, uncontrolled thyroid disease, poorly controlled diabetes, neurological disorders, cervical spine pathology, and a long list of drugs from steroids and MAOIs to anticoagulants and lithium [9]. Causes of upper airway obstruction such as Ludwig's angina or submandibular cellulitis are not just contraindications but indications to secure the airway [10].

## Drug review before GA is part of the workup

MAOIs are stopped 2 weeks pre-GA, antiepileptics are continued through, antihypertensives and bronchodilators are continued with the anaesthetist informed, lithium is checked and omitted before major surgery, and oral anticoagulants are stopped and the patient heparinised with INR or KCT monitoring [11]. The pattern is consistent: most chronic medications stay, a small list comes off, and the anaesthetist is told either way.

## Monitoring is now standard but does not replace clinical observation

Minimum monitoring set by the Royal College of Anaesthetists is BP, ECG, SaO2, and end-tidal CO2 [12]. These do not replace the anaesthetist's eyes on pulse, colour, skin changes, and breathing pattern, they support them [12].

citations.quote: General anaesthesia is a triad of unconsciousness, muscle relaxation, and analgesia.

The fundamental problem for any dental, oral, or maxillofacial anaesthetic is that the surgeon and anaesthetist both need to have access to the same anatomical site: the shared airway. The means by which this is overcome in hospital practice is usually by endotracheal, particularly nasoendotracheal, intubation, muscle relaxation, and ventilation.
The major risk of intubation is intubating the oesophagus and not recognizing it.

Patients must be starved as it does not protect against aspiration. It occupies a substantial volume in the mouth. The necessity of movement of the LMA to allow surgical access may displace the cuff, possibly causing laryngeal obstruction.
Since the GDC’s 2001 amendment to Maintaining Standards: General Anaesthesia and Resuscitation, the administration of GAs in dental practice setting has been effectively abolished in the UK.

Dental treatment under GA should only be carried out when it is judged to be the most clinically appropriate method of anaesthesia; and only take place in a hospital setting that has critical-care facilities.

GA may only be given by someone who is on the specialist register of the General Medical Council as an anaesthetist; a trainee working under supervision as part of a Royal College of Anaesthetists’ approved training programme; or a non-consultant career-grade anaesthetist with an NHS appointment under the supervision of a named consultant anaesthetist, who must be a member of the same NHS anaesthetic department where the non-consultant career-grade anaesthetist is employed.
Presence of food or fluid in the stomach (most anaesthetists require at least 6h fasting after food and 4h after fluid).

Cardiovascular or respiratory disease (especially MI <6 months ago). Uncorrected anaemia, sickle cell trait or disease. Severe liver or renal impairment. Uncontrolled thyrotoxicosis or hypothyroidism. Poorly controlled diabetes, adrenocortical suppression. Porphyria. Pregnancy. Neurological disorders, e.g. myopathy or multiple sclerosis. Cervical spine pathology such as rheumatoid arthritis or cervical spondylosis. Certain drugs, e.g. steroids, antihypertensives, MAOIs, anticoagulants, narcotic analgesics, antiepileptics (need to avoid using methohexital), lithium, alcohol.

Causes of upper airway obstruction such as angio-oedema, submandibular cellulitis, Ludwig’s angina, and bleeding diathesis affecting the neck. (In fact, these are indications to secure the upper airway.)
Should be stopped 2 weeks prior to GA.

It must be stressed, however, that these machines do not replace, only i, the ability of the anaesthetist to use clinical observation of pulse, colour, skin changes, and ventilatory pattern. Minimum standard of monitoring in the UK set by Royal College of Anaesthetists is BP, ECG, SaO2, and end-tidal CO2.
